source.title: Investigating the impact of low to moderate level label noise on Neural Network grokking dynamics

page_placements.theme: Label noise changes timing, fitting order and recovery

record.tranche_reason: The study trains MLPs on modular addition and measures delayed generalization, using training and test accuracy over training. It varies training-label noise rather than training-set size.
record.gate_note: The study explicitly reports that all 155 main-experiment runs grokked, defined as training accuracy reaching ≥ 95% and test accuracy later reaching within 5% of training accuracy. Rows record total epochs to grok, the most direct reported measure of delay. The Grokking Index and Loss Index are also reported, but are left out under the 60-row cap; cited results and proposed mechanistic explanations are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains an MLP on (a+b) mod 97 and tracks train and test accuracy until test catches up. This bears directly on V1's delayed generalization. The new factor is training-label noise (0–15%), plus weight-decay and learning-rate ablations. It is a new setting on the canonical task rather than a same-method replication: it uses an MLP rather than a transformer and does not vary training-set size.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that in their modular-addition MLP setup, training-label noise exponentially increases time to grok and the generalization gap. Even 0.5% noise hurts, and there is no beneficial regularization effect. All 155 main runs grokked up to 15% noise. They present exponential scaling as robust across splits and the stable configurations (Original, WD_0.5), while WD_2.0, LR_1e-3 and LR_1e-2 are boundary cases poorly matched to the task.
record.recipe_differences: Uses modular addition and training/test accuracy to study grokking, but uses an MLP on (a + b) mod 97, a 40/60 split, and systematic training-label-noise sweeps; also varies weight decay and learning rate in ablations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported delay varies with training-label-noise level, weight decay, learning rate, and random train-test split. The authors report exponential scaling for configurations they describe as reliably grokking, with boundary cases under other optimization settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Uniform training-label noise lengthens time to grok and the train–test gap roughly exponentially. The fit is Total Epochs = 411.6·e^(0.235·noise%), R²=0.855. Even 0.5% noise measurably delays grokking.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training-label noise lengthens the grokking delay, approximately exponentially in noise rate.

fits_no_version.finding: Higher weight decay (2.0) or learning rate (0.01) removes the delay at low noise, while lower weight decay (0.5) or learning rate (0.001) lengthens it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The size of the grokking delay on modular addition is controlled by weight decay and learning rate.

record.problems: The primary experiment has five runs per noise level. The authors note increased run-to-run variability at high noise and local non-monotonicity. Evidence is specific to modular addition, one MLP architecture, a 40/60 split, and uniform random training-label corruption. The study does not vary training-set size or directly analyze internal circuits.
record.rows_left_out: Under the 60-row cap, retained total-epoch outcomes and omitted Grokking Index and Loss Index results from Tables 11 and 13. From Table 12, retained total-epoch outcomes at 0%, 5%, and 15% noise for each split; omitted the separately reported 10% noise total-epoch outcomes. The hyperparameter-ablation total-epoch values are all retained.

untested.parts: Training-set size is fixed at 40%, so the claim that the delay grows as the training set shrinks is untested. A start at chance-level test accuracy is not reported numerically.
No circuit analysis or progress measures that could anticipate the jump.
No non-algorithmic data, initialization-scale sweep or lazy-to-rich analysis. Weight decay is varied only on modular addition.
No efficiency, critical dataset size or ungrokking tests.
Learned algorithms are not identified or compared.
Optimizer instabilities and softmax numerics are not examined; only AdamW is used.

missing.what: Per-run epochs of 95% train accuracy versus test catch-up, which give the delay directly: 334→608 (0%), 363→882 (5%), 412→2347 (10%)

record.verdict_notes: The rows' measure, 'total epochs to grok', includes the memorization phase and does not isolate the delay. The Grokking Index (Tables 11 and 13) shows whether a delay exists, and it is near zero for WD_2.0 and LR_1e-2 at ≤10% noise, so those rows were changed from observed to absent. The clean-data delay is far smaller than in Power et al. Rows r52, r55 and r56 sit at the 50,000-epoch cap. The paper is a high-school journal article with n=5 per condition. Its mechanistic explanations (hypothesis-space explosion) are speculative and not tested.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not vary training-set size, so it does not test whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks. It reports grokking by an accuracy threshold, but does not give numeric chance-level test accuracy or detailed training/test accuracy trajectories for every run.
No generalizing circuit is identified or tracked, and the study does not test whether continuous mechanism measures anticipate an accuracy jump.
No non-algorithmic dataset or initialization-scale sweep is tested. Weight decay and learning rate are varied, but the study does not test a lazy-to-rich transition.
No realistic large-model pretraining or fine-tuning is tested.
The study does not test circuit efficiency, norm preference, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below such a size.
The study does not identify or compare learned algorithms across runs.
The study does not investigate adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point limits in the softmax as explanations for grokking.

relationships.condition: Main configuration (WD 1.0, LR 5e-3) at all noise levels 0–15%, the three independent splits, and the Original and WD_0.5 ablation configurations
relationships.reason: Every run reached ≥95% train accuracy first and generalized later (r01–r48). In the clean sample run, train accuracy hit 95% at epoch 334 and test caught up at 608, so the delay is modest (under 2× memorization time).
relationships.display_finding: Every run reached at least 95% training accuracy before generalizing, and the clean example reached 95% training accuracy at epoch 334 and test accuracy at epoch 608, under twice the memorization time.

source_check.reason: Section 3.1 reports delayed generalization in all 155 main runs; Tables 12–13 and accompanying text report the same behavior across splits and the two stable configurations. The clean example reaches 95% training accuracy at epoch 334 and the test catch-up criterion at 608. Training-set-size dependence is untested.

relationships.condition: WD 2.0 or LR 1e-2 at 0–10% noise; WD 2.0 and LR 1e-3 at high noise
relationships.reason: The delay depends on optimizer settings. Grokking Index is about 0 with near-instant generalization (r49–r51, r57–r59), and runs hit the 50k cap without grokking (r52, r55, r56). LR_1e-2 at 15% is inconsistent (r60). This rests on Table 13's Grokking Index, which the rows omit.
relationships.display_finding: Some settings gave a Grokking Index near zero and nearly immediate generalization, others failed to grok within 50,000 steps, and learning rate 0.01 behaved inconsistently at 15% noise.

source_check.notes: The reported uncertainties are standard deviations across five runs. Grokking uses ≥95% training accuracy followed by test accuracy within 5 percentage points; r52 records a training cap, and the fixed 40/60 split leaves training-set-size dependence untested.

reader_labels.condition: Main MLP configuration across 0%–15% training-label noise, and the sampled independent-split conditions
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that all 155 main runs grokked; total epochs generally rose with noise, and the independent-split results also show longer delays at higher tested noise (r01–r40). This supports delayed generalization in the tested algorithmic setup, but does not test the claim's training-set-size relationship.
